blocks.prompt: The Suit With a Hundred Pieces
blocks.text: A knight's metal suit was called armor. It was not one piece. It was made of many pieces that all fit together. There were metal shoes for his feet. There were metal gloves for his hands. There was a helmet with a flap that lifted up so he could see. Every piece was made to fit one knight only, like a pair of shoes made just for you. The helmet hid his face. So the knight painted a pattern on his shield. His friends knew the pattern. That way they could find him in a crowd.

blocks.prompt: Fourteen Years to Become a Knight
blocks.text: In much of medieval Europe, no one became a knight in a day. It took about fourteen years, and it started when you were seven. At seven, a boy was sent away to live in another lord's castle. He was called a page. He carried messages, waited at the table, and learned to look after horses. He practiced sword moves with a wooden sword. At about fourteen, he became a squire. A squire belonged to one knight. He cleaned the knight's armor, saddled his war horse, and carried his shield. When the knight rode to battle, the squire rode behind him and watched. At about twenty-one, if he had done well, he was made a knight. The ceremony was short. A lord tapped him on the shoulder with the flat of a sword, and it was done. He had spent most of his childhood getting ready for that tap.

notes: A full suit weighed about fifty pounds

blocks.prompt: The Beetle on Its Back, and Why It Is Wrong
blocks.text: You have probably seen the scene in a movie. A knight in shining armor is so weighed down by steel that he can barely waddle, and when he falls over he lies there like an upturned beetle until someone hauls him up with a crane. It is a good joke. It is also wrong. A full suit of field armor from the 1400s weighed about fifty pounds. That sounds like a lot until you notice where the weight sat. Armor was strapped to the whole body, so the arm pieces rode on the arms and the leg pieces rode on the legs. Nothing hung off the shoulders. A modern soldier often carries more than that in a single pack, and all of it pulls down on the back. Knights in armor could run. They could climb into the saddle without help. They could get up off the ground. They had to, because a knight who could not stand up was a dead knight. Before plate armor, knights wore mail: thousands of small iron rings, each one linked through four others, punched and riveted shut by hand. A mail shirt could hold thirty thousand rings. It took an armorer months. Plate armor was fitted to one body, like a suit of clothes made of steel. It had hinges at the elbow and knee and overlapping plates at the shoulder so the joints still bent. The best armorers in Milan and Augsburg were famous, and rich knights waited years for their work.

notes: Knights paid for their own armor and horses

blocks.prompt: Who Paid for the Shining Armor
blocks.text: Here is a question that storybooks never ask: who paid for all that steel? The knight did. A knight supplied his own armor, his own weapons, and his own horses, and the bill was staggering. The armor alone could cost more than a farm worker earned in several years. The horse cost more than the armor. A destrier, the heavy war horse bred to carry an armored man at a charge, was the single most expensive animal in medieval Europe, and a knight needed more than one, because horses go lame and horses die. Add a squire, a groom, spare weapons, and food for all of them, and you can see why knights came from families that already owned land. Being a knight was not a job you applied for. It was a job you could afford. That expense shaped everything, including the tournament. Tournaments began as mock battles called melees, in which two teams of knights fought across open countryside for hours. Men were injured. Men died. The prize was not a trophy. A winner could capture a beaten knight's horse and armor and demand a ransom to give them back, which meant a skilled young knight with no land could actually make a living on the tournament circuit. Later, the joust became the showpiece: two riders, one fence, one lance each. It was safer, but not safe. In 1559, King Henry II of France took a lance splinter through the slot in his visor and died ten days later. And chivalry? Chivalry was the code knights were supposed to live by: courage, loyalty, mercy to the beaten, protection for the weak. Some knights took it seriously. Many did not. During the Hundred Years' War, English knights ran raids called chevauchees, riding through French countryside and deliberately burning farms, mills, and villages to wreck the enemy king's income. The same men who swore to protect the helpless were paid to ruin them. So the storybook knight is not a lie, exactly. He is a highlight reel. The code was real, the courage was often real, and so were the burned villages and the ransom bills.

meta.templateLabel: The Knight Who Started Out as a Kid

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Crecy 1346 and Agincourt 1415
Swiss pike blocks stopped cavalry charges
Proof mark: a dent left by a test shot
Leeds 2011: armor doubled the energy cost of running
Cniht is Old English for boy or servant
Britain still knights people today

blocks.prompt: The Knight Was Killed by Arithmetic
blocks.text: For roughly four hundred years, a man in steel on a heavy horse was the most powerful thing on a European battlefield. Then, over about a century and a half, he stopped being worth the money. That second sentence is the interesting one, because the knight did not lose a fight with a better weapon. He lost an argument with a ledger. Start with what actually worked against him. At Crecy in 1346 and again at Agincourt in 1415, English longbowmen broke French cavalry charges. The longbow did not punch cleanly through good plate at a distance, and the story that it did is mostly wishful. What it did was kill horses, wound the badly armored, and turn a charge into a jam of stalled men in churned mud, where they could be finished off on foot. Around the same time, Swiss infantry proved something even more upsetting: a tight block of ordinary men holding long pikes could stop a cavalry charge dead, and those men cost almost nothing to equip. Then gunpowder arrived, and armorers did the obvious thing. They made the steel thicker. Fifteenth and sixteenth century breastplates got heavier and were sometimes tested by firing a gun at them, leaving a dent called a proof mark that was a receipt: this plate stopped a ball. It worked. It also could not scale. Armor thick enough to defeat a musket everywhere would be too heavy to move in, so armor retreated. It shrank to a helmet and a breastplate, and then to almost nothing. Here is the arithmetic. One knight took fourteen years to train, starting at age seven. He supplied armor and multiple war horses at a price only a landholding family could carry. An arquebusier could be handed a gun and taught to use it in weeks, and a hundred of them cost less than a handful of knights. Kings noticed. As they got richer and better at collecting taxes, they stopped begging vassals to show up with their own gear and started paying professional soldiers who showed up because it was their job. The whole feudal machine that produced knights, land in exchange for service, quietly became a worse deal than cash. So the knight did not die. He was outbid. What survived is the word. In Britain, the monarch still knights people, and the ceremony is a light touch of a sword on each shoulder, a direct descendant of the medieval accolade. Nobody expects the new knight to own a horse. The title got separated from the job that made it, and then it outlived the job by four hundred years, which is a strange kind of afterlife for a word that started in Old English as cniht, meaning boy, or servant. There is one last fact worth holding on to. In 2011, researchers at the University of Leeds put volunteers in accurate replica fifteenth century armor and ran them on a treadmill while measuring their oxygen use. Wearing the armor roughly doubled the energy cost of walking and running. Part of that was the weight on the legs, and part was the breastplate itself, which made deep breathing hard. So the knight was not a slow beetle in a can, as the movies pretend. He was an athlete doing everything twice as hard as you would, for fourteen years of training, in a suit that his family had to sell land to buy.
